case_info.scenario: A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Interaction Guidelines]

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.

            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
case_info.caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
case_info.explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
